t: Together, we, the working surgeons of the world, will institute the Pax Inguinalis, a just and equitable anatomic peace that will eliminate the burden of post hernia repair pain syndromes.
As chief negotiator, I embark on this effort without weighty professorial or academic credentials.
The hallmark of my curriculum vitae is a 40-year membership in the Automobile Club of Southern California,
as well as a rather well-received after-dinner speech in Morristown, New Jersey in 2002.
I have never published scientific papers on inguinal hernia repair.
I have no academic rank or surgical prestige.
I have never opined on when the transversus abdominis becomes a ponerotic,
although I dated a woman once who became a Ponerotic during an anti-war rally in Chicago in 1971.
But that's for another essay.
I have eschewed the faculty lounge, the breakout session, and the focus group.
I once, however, had a brief liaison with a facilitator.
Because I lack academic gravitas, I am doubly honored to have been chosen
from the surgical rank and file to serve as chief negotiator.
My single qualification for moderating the negotiations for the Pax Inguinalis is that
I have performed a lot of hernia repairs. I have also been confronted with just about
every conceivable complication of this operation. In addition, I have chaired
many conference reviews of complications of hernia repair. Many of these complications
arose after what I thought had been well-performed surgical procedures.
But any experienced surgeon realizes that complications can occur after even well-performed
procedures.
Surgery is biology.
Surgery is not chemistry.
Every time one mixes oxygen and hydrogen under the proper circumstances, one will
get water.
Not so in surgery, where every time a well-performed hernia repair is carried out, perfection
does not necessarily ensue.
I repaired a right inguinal hernia on Sid Rosenthal.
Sid Rosenthal's testicle became a grapefruit.
I repaired Maury Klein's recurrent left inguinal hernia.
Maury Klein's hernia recurred.
Phil Fleiber's hematoma took two months to resolve.
Sylvia Plathman-Nirdlinger's left labium majus
was numb for six months.
Kyle Fuhrman's testicle atrophied after repair
of a recurrent hernia three months before his wedding.
And I have not even mentioned Jan Klosterman's year-long John Wayne gait.
I have traveled down that canal.
In addition to a litany of my own post-operative problems, I have also seen many patients
in second opinion consultation.
I have seen these patients on a pre-operative visit and in second opinion during a post-operative
visit.
But even recognizing the potential complications of this procedure, I continue to enjoy the
the surgical challenge of hernia repair.
I have discussed all these aspects of repair for many years
with a group of well-educated and experienced colleagues.
These comments and insights have not been published
as tracks in Acta Herniographica, Scandinavica,
or even in annals of herniology.
They have not been subjected
to the Kaplan-Meier regression analysis.
They have not been scrutinized
by an institutional review board committee.
My observations have weathered
the unyielding tripartite crucible of the surgeon's lounge,
the physician's dining area,
and legions of inquisitive
and sometimes quite annoying surgical residents
prior to their commencing laudable careers
in dermatology.
Inguinal hernia repair,
and I limit my comments here to standard,
inguinal hernia repair,
is a marvelous exercise in anatomic precision,
human embryology, surgical history, and operative technique.
When I gaze at the freshly-shaven,
inguinal region laid bare after the timeout,
review of the surgical team's
tuberculin test status, checklist,
operating theater code of conduct,
conflict of interest, disclaimer,
and underwriter's laboratory history
of the electrocautery unit,
I think of, and will express to any resident
permitted to be present by work hour requirements,
the following issues and insights.
One, what life events
has this inguinal region experienced?
Two, who was president of the United States
when this inguinal region was created?
Three, did this inguinal region
ever see military combat?
Four, does this region realize
that it houses Hesselbach's triangle,
Tisdale's trapezoid, the dorodecahedron of de Monde,
Onan's octagon, a processus vaginalis and vaginalis,
filamentous chromaster fibers, and a Pampinaform plexus.
Why is the plexus called Pampinaform?
This will be covered in a breakout session on day two.
Five, does this inguinal region realize
that despite strict zoning laws,
that it lives close to at least 17 other tubercles?
Six, who came through this vas deferens?
Who was supported by this round ligament?
Whatever happened to these individuals?
Seven, has this inguinal area ever been swimming
in Lake Winnipesaukee in early June
and been surprised by a vigorous dartos reflex?
Eight, where was this inguinal area
when the Red Sox won the World Series?
Nine, where was this inguinal area
when the Cubs won the World Series?
Ten, is this inguinal region aware of Maimonides' seminal text on the descent of the Kishkis?
All parties at the negotiating table understand our initial task for a just and lasting peace
in the inguinal region begins with a discussion of the issues that arise before the operation.
And it is on this front where my formidable negotiating skills will bring together two
warring surgical camps.
Stay tuned for part 3, where I discuss whether the benefits of the repair outweigh the risks
of the repair.
